title: How to End the Iran War
gist: Two Atlantic Council Iran hands argue the U.S.-Iran war is a sunk-cost trap in which American leverage decays weekly, and that the only available exit is a narrow deal trading permanent oil-sanctions relief (an open-ended General License X) for a U.N.-supervised Strait of Hormuz transit mechanism that formalizes but constrains Iran's new control of the waterway. They warn that without U.S. coordination, competing European, Gulf and Saudi-Pakistani initiatives will let Tehran shop for the best deal.

themes.theme: Decaying U.S. leverage in the Iran war

insights.claim: U.S. negotiating leverage against Iran has diminished as the war has progressed and will keep eroding as American munitions stocks are exhausted and domestic political consequences mount.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Time is not on Washington's side: expect the terms of any eventual settlement to get worse for the U.S. and better for Iran the longer the conflict runs, which argues for pricing in a concessionary deal rather than an Iranian capitulation.
insights.quote: In reality, U.S. negotiating leverage has diminished as the war has progressed and will likely continue to erode as the United States exhausts its munitions and domestic political consequences mount.
insights.locator: As Washington and Tehran trade messages

insights.claim: The Trump administration has repeatedly fallen prey to the sunk cost fallacy in the Iran war, treating a strategic failure as if it were merely a problem of scale or duration.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Escalation rather than de-escalation is the administration's default reflex, so risk models should weight further intensification higher than a clean exit.
insights.quote: The administration has repeatedly fallen prey to the sunk cost fallacy.
insights.locator: As Washington and Tehran trade messages

insights.claim: Nearly five decades of U.S. military, economic and political pressure have failed to bend Iran, and pressure has only shaped Iranian decision-making when paired with inducements, coalitions, mutual respect and patience.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Maximum-pressure-only policy paths have a five-decade failure record; deals that include real economic inducements are the ones with a chance of durably reopening Iranian oil flows.
insights.quote: There is a myth in Washington that pressure alone can break Iran.
insights.locator: There is a myth in Washington

insights.claim: Although the United States remains the superior conventional military power, Iran's political will to continue the war is stronger, so both capitals treat negotiations as surrender while disagreeing over who is surrendering.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Cease-fire headlines will keep collapsing until a deal is structured so both sides can claim victory — fade one-sided 'Iran capitulates' narratives.
insights.quote: The result is that Washington and Tehran both treat negotiations as surrender—while disagreeing over who is doing the surrendering.
insights.locator: The key to any sustainable deal

insights.claim: Ambiguity in sections 4 and 5 of the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding, which addressed the Strait of Hormuz, made the cease-fire inherently fragile and contributed to its collapse because each side could credibly blame the other for non-compliance.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Cease-fire durability hinges on the specificity of the Hormuz transit language, not on the headline announcement — read the text before repricing tanker rates or crude risk premia.
insights.quote: Ambiguity in sections 4 and 5, which addressed the Strait of Hormuz, made the cease-fire inherently fragile and ultimately contributed to its collapse.
insights.locator: The MOU between the United States and Iran

insights.claim: Decision-making in both Washington and Tehran is driven more by short-term domestic perceptions than long-term strategic gains, and influential constituencies in each capital actively oppose a diplomatic solution.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Deal timing will track electoral and factional calendars rather than battlefield logic; watch U.S. midterms and Iranian internal politics as the real catalysts.
insights.locator: Second, decision-making in both countries

insights.claim: Section 9 of the U.S.-Iran MOU commits Iran to maintaining the status quo of its nuclear program, and as a result of the 12-day war in June 2025 Iran is currently neither enriching uranium nor building new centrifuges.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: The nuclear clock is frozen, which gives Washington the luxury of patience and removes near-term breakout risk from the tail-risk stack even while the shooting war continues.
insights.quote: As a result of the 12-day war in June 2025, Iran is not currently enriching uranium or building new centrifuges.
insights.locator: Section 9 of the MOU

insights.claim: A majority of Iran's leading decision-makers supported the June memorandum of understanding and understand that the war cannot continue indefinitely, despite powerful domestic entities favoring its continuation.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: There is a real Iranian constituency for a deal, so cease-fire optionality is higher than hardline rhetoric implies.
insights.locator: There are certainly powerful entities in Iran

insights.claim: The workable bargain is that the United States ends attacks, lifts the blockade and reissues General License X authorizing Iranian oil sales with no specified end date, in exchange for Iranian cooperation on unobstructed passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: An open-ended General License X would be a structural bearish shock to crude by legitimizing Iranian barrels permanently rather than temporarily; watch Treasury OFAC actions as the tradeable signal.
insights.quote: The general license would stay in effect as long as Iran avoids any obstruction over the passage of ships.
insights.locator: The parties could achieve these objectives

insights.claim: The Trump administration has already issued General License X twice on a temporary basis, so making it permanent is a concession Washington has effectively pre-conceded.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: The political cost of permanent Iranian oil-sanctions relief is lower than headlines suggest, raising the probability of the bearish-crude scenario.
insights.locator: This is a meaningful and permanent economic concession

insights.claim: Any Hormuz mechanism must avoid two specific failure modes: creating a precedent that undermines freedom of navigation elsewhere, and letting Tehran use administrative control over ship passage to extract continual concessions from the Gulf.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: If a deal grants Iran fee or toll authority over transits, expect a permanent structural premium on Gulf shipping and insurance and copycat chokepoint claims elsewhere.
insights.locator: The key U.S. objective should be to avoid

insights.claim: Omani officials proposed to Iran a purely regional body to oversee maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz, but such a body is vulnerable to intraregional disputes and its security mandate could provide cover for aggression in the waterway.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Headlines about an Omani-brokered regional maritime body should be read as fragile, not as a durable de-risking of the chokepoint.
insights.locator: Omani officials were in Iran over the weekend

insights.claim: The proposed alternative is a U.N.-auspices mechanism including Iran, Oman and a rotating Gulf seat that remotely monitors strait traffic and settles transit disputes, enshrining Iran's leading role while constraining unilateral obstruction and making tolls or fees unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: A U.N. monitoring body with no fee regime is the outcome most bearish for freight-rate and war-risk premia in the Gulf; a fee-based regional body is the most bullish.
insights.locator: Muscat and regional mediators should instead propose

insights.claim: A small Hormuz deal is a prerequisite for a future nuclear deal because neither side currently believes the other can meet its commitments, and Washington still holds the big incentives — access to global banking, trade and investment — in reserve.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Sequencing matters: a narrow shipping agreement is the leading indicator to watch before positioning for full Iranian reintegration into global banking and trade.
insights.locator: A small deal on Hormuz may also increase the odds

insights.claim: Iran's most effective wartime strategy has been striking U.S. partners directly — countries that host energy, digital and economic infrastructure vital to the global economy — rather than attacking American forces.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Gulf energy and data-center infrastructure is the actual target set; price physical-asset and insurance risk in the GCC rather than only in the strait itself.
insights.locator: Beyond the strait, Iran’s most effective wartime strategy

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are already reducing dependence on the Strait of Hormuz through new pipelines and port expansions, while Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar lack similar outlets.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Qatari LNG and Kuwaiti and Bahraini crude carry undiversifiable chokepoint exposure that Saudi and Emirati barrels do not — a clear relative-risk discriminator across Gulf exporters.
insights.locator: It also means new trade and energy infrastructure

insights.claim: U.S. equipment alone cannot resupply Gulf air defenses, forcing Washington to embrace layered integrated air defense built in collaboration with European and Asian partners.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Gulf air-defense procurement is opening to European and Asian suppliers out of sheer capacity constraints — a durable order-book tailwind beyond U.S. primes.
insights.quote: Because U.S. equipment alone cannot resupply Gulf air defenses, this means embracing layered, integrated air defense built in collaboration with European and Asian partners.
insights.locator: Because U.S. equipment alone cannot resupply

insights.claim: New Houthi attacks on Saudi oil exports add fresh precarity to a war that has already induced global economic shocks and damaged U.S. credibility.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Saudi export infrastructure is an active target independent of the Hormuz question, so a strait deal alone would not clear the oil-supply risk premium.
insights.locator: New Houthi attacks on Saudi oil exports

insights.claim: If Washington keeps treating any Gulf engagement with Iran as a threat, Gulf partners will pursue engagement strategies that undermine U.S. policy, such as facilitating sanctions evasion.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Sanctions leakage through Gulf financial and trading channels is the predictable byproduct of U.S. rigidity — a compliance risk for regional banks and commodity traders.
insights.locator: Washington tends to view any Gulf engagement with Iran

themes.theme: Middle-power initiatives filling the U.S. vacuum

insights.claim: Because the United States failed to secure the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom and France have stood up a maritime initiative involving some 40 countries to potentially manage post-cease-fire security operations there, without Washington at the table.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: European navies, not the U.S. Fifth Fleet, may end up setting the post-cease-fire escort regime — a structural shift in who underwrites Gulf shipping security.
insights.quote: the United Kingdom and France have stood up a maritime initiative involving some 40 countries to potentially manage post-cease-fire security operations there—without Washington at the table
insights.locator: In the absence of U.S. leadership

insights.claim: A senior European diplomat told the authors that Europe has fielded more calls from Gulf leaders in the past few months than in the previous decade.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Gulf capitals are actively diversifying their security patron away from Washington, which over time reshapes defense procurement, energy contracts and reserve-currency preferences.
insights.quote: A senior European diplomat recently told us that they’ve fielded more calls from Gulf leaders in the past few months than in the previous decade.
insights.locator: In the absence of U.S. leadership

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has proposed a regional security dialogue with Iran and is exploring whether a deeper partnership with Pakistan can help shape Iranian behavior.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: A Saudi-Pakistan security deepening is a live nuclear-adjacent hedge in the Gulf and a variable to track for South Asian and Gulf risk alike.
insights.locator: The Gulf itself is moving, too

insights.claim: Uncoordinated middle-power initiatives on Iran would produce strategic incoherence and let Tehran shop around for the best deal while sowing discord among the United States and its partners.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Fragmented Western and Gulf diplomacy raises the probability of a bad or unstable settlement, keeping a persistent geopolitical premium in energy and shipping.
insights.quote: It would allow Iran to shop around for the best deal while sowing discord among the United States and its partners.
insights.locator: However, in the absence of coordination

insights.claim: Gulf capitals complain that Washington treats them like ATMs, failing to consult them on major Middle East policy decisions while mining them for resources to manage the consequences.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Gulf sovereign capital deployment into U.S. political priorities is increasingly conditional, a headwind for U.S.-directed Gulf investment pledges.
insights.quote: Gulf capitals have long complained that Washington treats them like ATMs
insights.locator: One of the most dangerous assumptions about Iran

insights.claim: The available version of victory is a deal that reopens the Strait of Hormuz, avoids further harm to U.S. allies and retains the freeze on Iran's nuclear program — not Iranian unconditional surrender, which was never achievable.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: The realistic base case is a modest, face-saving settlement that reopens shipping without resolving the nuclear file — plan for partial rather than clean risk-off resolution.
insights.quote: The war was never going to end with Iran’s unconditional surrender.
insights.locator: That is what ending the war requires

insights.claim: A quick-win Iran deal designed mainly to bring down U.S. gasoline prices before the midterm elections would be too shallow to be durable and risks setting a dangerous freedom-of-navigation precedent.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: A pre-midterm cease-fire headline may compress the oil risk premium temporarily while leaving the structural chokepoint risk intact — a candidate for fading the initial move.
insights.quote: But this requires more than inking a quick-win deal to bring down gas prices before the U.S. midterm elections.
insights.locator: Ultimately, both sides should have strong motivations

insights.claim: Every additional day of war and every destroyed bridge or business lengthens the road to economic recovery for an Iranian regime that was already facing existential political and economic challenges before the conflict began.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor, Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Iranian reconstruction and the associated capital needs will be a multi-year story even in a best-case settlement, capping how fast Iranian supply and demand normalize.
insights.quote: But to end the war, Iranian leaders need to believe that recovery is possible.
insights.locator: Yet even as Tehran’s position hardens
